Question: What you need next to transition from classical thermodynamics to quantum thermodynamics is a transformation matrix from velocity (not momentum because I don't believe in mass but believe in matter) to frequency or wavelength?
Answer: There is a procedure called canonical quantization which is used to transform a classical theory into a quantum theory. It’s basically a “recipe,” and as far as I can tell it works well. One thing worth noting is that part of this procedure is the deliberate injection of uncertainty into the theory - quantum mechanics doesn’t “prove” the uncertainty principle. Rather, we build uncertainty in on purpose, because we studied the world and started to believe that uncertainty between certain pairs of variables was just part of it. So we designed the mathematics such that it would produce that uncertainty. Keep in mind also that quantum theory is not a theory about “what happens in the world.” In fact, it deliberately hides from us a lot of the details - it’s not clear whether those details even actually exist or not. Quantum mechanics is a theory about what we expect our measurement results to be. So the concept of “observer,” and “measurement,” and “instrument” are deeply embedded in the whole program. The program doesn’t make sense without them. This bothers a lot of people, but… it’s what we’ve got right now. Stay safe and well! Question: Is wave-particle duality applicable to large objects like planets and stars? Can they also be considered as both waves and particles simultaneously?
Answer: People tend to attach too much significance to the wave/particle thing. What quantum mechanics actually tells us is the probability of getting particular measurement results. That is all. There is a mathematical procedure for calculating those results, and those results are numbers. Whether something “wave like” or “particle like” has happened is largely a matter of interpretation - the theory doesn’t deal in things like “wave mode” or “particle mode” that things flip back and forth between. Also, wave functions don’t exist in physical space. You should think of them as existing in a “space of possible measurement results.” If you happen to be measuring the position of a single particle, then it’s easy enough to squint and pretend you’re talking about something in physical space, but you’re really not, and in other cases it’s not even close - the wave function may not even occupy a three-dimensional space. It just depends on what it is you’re measuring and how complicated your quantum system is. When the wave function “collapses” as a result of a measurement, there is no “physics” associated with that - no “process.” You just look at what the result of your measurement was and manually and arbitrarily discard the previously existing wave function and substitute in a new one. It’s really more of a “cheat” than it is anything else. You now know things you didn’t know before, so you can rule out wave functions that don’t correspond to your new knowledge. Quantum mechanics is not a theory about “what happens in the world.” It’s a theory about what we should expect our measurement results to be. Consequently, the notions of observer, measurement, instrument, and so on are “baked into it” in an inextricable way. This bothers a lot of people (Tim Maudlin springs to mind), but it’s how it is. Question: Is there any visible light from the Big Bang or just radiation? If there is visible light, what color would it be and why? If not, how do we know that the Big Bang occurred?
Answer: No, the leftovers of the Big Bang have red-shifted out of the frequency range directly visible to our eyes. And you’re very glad of that too - if the whole sky was shining in the visible light range, then you’d burn up in short order. However, you seem to feel that unless you can see it with your eye you’re not willing to believe it exists. That’s fairly ridiculous - that electromagnetic radiation is still there, and we can see it no matter what direction we look using suitable instrumentation. The necessity of an instrument does not in any way make the radiation less real. Stay safe and well!
